# Porto Notes

## Overview

Four nights in Porto in late spring, in a third-floor flat above a bakery on the Ribeira side of the centre. The river was ten minutes downhill, which meant ten minutes uphill on the way back, and my legs noticed by the second day. I came without much of a plan and let the town set the pace. The weather ran warm and bright most afternoons, cool at night, with one squall that emptied the quayside in a minute.

I walked the bridge to the far bank twice, once at sunset and once early, and the two crossings felt like different towns. The metro from the airport takes half an hour to the centre and costs about 2.50 EUR with the card fee on top. Trams rattle past the cathedral and up the hill toward the sea, and I took one to the coast on the last morning. The tiled churches and the iron market hall were the buildings I kept returning to, and the hilltop square gave the best view of the roofs. I paid 70 EUR a night for the flat, which felt fair for the location. The tiled façade of the station is worth the five minutes it takes to look up, and I passed it most mornings on the way uphill. I would come back in the spring again and stay on the same side of the river.

## Food

The food here is heavy in the best way, and I ate well every day. The market is the place to start, a two-tier hall near the river where the ground floor sells produce and the upper floor turns it into lunches. I had grilled sardines from a stall there, four on a plate with bread, for about 9 EUR, and the smell of charcoal followed me all afternoon. The fish come in early summer and the stalls cook them whole, salted and crisp, best eaten with the fingers.

I booked a cellar tour one afternoon, about 15 EUR, on the far bank in Vila Nova de Gaia, and it ended with a tasting of three ports, a white, a tawny and a ruby. The guide walked us through the long halls of barrels and explained how the river once carried the wine down in flat boats. It was the most useful hour of the trip for understanding what the town is for. I ate francesinha twice, a wet sandwich with a beer sauce, ham, sausage and a blanket of melted cheese, and it defeated me both times; 12 EUR at a plain café near the station was the better of the two. A slow dinner of grilled octopus and rice came to 20 EUR, and the bakery below the flat supplied breakfast for 3 EUR. Cheese boards and cured ham are worth a lunch on their own, and a plate of both with bread came to 14 EUR at a shop in the arcade. I drank the local vinho verde with the sardines, light and slightly fizzy, a glass for 3 EUR. Coffee here comes small and strong, 0.80 EUR at the counter, and I took two a day. The pastries are heavy and sweet, custard and almond mostly, and one with coffee made a cheap breakfast standing at the bar.

## Notes

The riverfront is quieter in the morning and the crowds arrive with the first tour boats around ten. I bought a three-day transport card and used it enough to justify the cost, though the centre itself is walkable. The funicular up from the quay saves a steep climb of about ten minutes and costs a couple of euros. Bookshops and tiled halls draw queues, so I went to the famous one at opening on a weekday and still shared it with twenty people. Cash helped at the market stalls, cards worked everywhere else. One rainy afternoon I stayed in the market hall with a coffee and watched the river rise a little. Photography is banned in parts of the churches. I would come back in autumn and skip the summer crush at the quayside. The metro runs late and I used it to get home after dinners on the far side of the centre. Tipping is not expected and the bill often comes with a small cover charge for the bread. Sundays close many of the smaller shops, so I did my wandering to the river and the parks instead. English is widely spoken, and I never struggled to order or ask directions. The airport bus runs every twenty minutes and takes about thirty minutes to the centre, cheaper than the metro with its card fee.
